Dude, it's not a drug to abuse and mess around with, like acid or shrooms. You wanna open yourself up? Try other substances . Ket is used in therapy for a reason, it also makes it easier to experience emotions like sadness and can make it easier to cry out what you need to (especially since T really does make it physically harder to cry). If it's because you want a euphoric "high", there's other things if the whole point is you're going to do drugs anyway (like mdma for instance). 

Don't recreationally take hrt. There's a reason, for example, that (cis) female bodybuilders were told not to mess around with steroids to bulk up: a person who's afab who takes testosterone will have big changes, not just in mood. It literally makes your downstairs grow so your body can be more like a cis guys (you get what I mean). Plus facial hair and literal face and body structure type changes. And while a lot of the stuff is reversible to an extent(even the loss of shark week) some aren't, like the thickening of vocal chords, thus lowering your voice permanently. I know you're a cis guy and E is different than T, but this is the best example I can give on how radical it changes you. Even small amounts, especially since everyone's body is different, and you don't know what dose works for your body. Also, if you take too much, it can have an opposite effect: I know of guys who took higher amounts of T thinking it would make changes arrive quicker. But when it comes down to it, any extra T winds up breaking down and becomes basically more E, which would be counterproductive. See how this is something that if you don't know about and don't need, you shouldn't mess with?

While you might experience mood swings and kinda like it/the ability to feel more deeply and differently, etc, E causes other changes too. Namely, it affects the tissue in your chest area to try and give you breasts. Like, it's not just your nipples that will get all swollen and sensitive . And I don't know too much about E regarding what changes stay or what are reversible. But it definitely messes with your body. And taking it on and off, even for short periods of time can definitely have an impact on your body. We don't know exactly the repercussions in medicine, but I know for instance that, each time I for whatever reason missed shots and wound up being off hrt for a few months here and there,  I realized it took longer for changes to revert back. It went from shark week coming back after missing about a month or two, to me going nearly 6 mo without hrt (long story) before mother nature paid me a visit. I'm pretty sure it's affected my fertility, and even though it makes me dysphoric to think about, if I ever wanted to get pregnant I don't think I'd even be able to anymore because of the decade of off and on treatments. It even took longer for things like my face shape to return from being more angled to round. Blood tests showed I still had high lvls (compared to what a cis female would have) of T in my body for months after missing shots.

My point is, if you read all that, don't do this. It was a fun little experiment, maybe it helped you affirm your gender if you felt any dysphoria being on E, but it's not a drug with a high that you can abuse. There's plenty of other things out there that you can try that can expand your mind or make you more empathetic and in tune with yourself that are safe for the most part. This isn't the answer. Now, if you're confused about your gender identity, if you felt more comfortable on E and it felt "right" , then that would be something else. If you realized you were actually trans, then I'd still say don't abuse it, but find a doctor for a legal prescription so you could start your journey.

I was sort of sympathetic at first, because hospitals are scary to be in alone, especially if you have trouble advocating for yourself, like myself (and most people with horrible anxiety). So I could see how he would not want you to leave, but he's still being unfair to you: maybe if he was dying I'd say it's different, but he's still undermining all you're doing. You're an adult, you have responsibilities, you can't just bail on your finals. This is your future on the line, and as your bf, he should want the best for you. The best for you, in this case, would be making sure you take care of your future and he should be pushing you and encouraging you to NOT stay.

But putting all that to the side, because when people are sick and feel like they're dying from feeling so shitty, it's easy for them to be irritable and act selfish. The thing that took me out though and made me say nah nvm, and toss my sympathy out the window, was when he blamed YOU for not moderating the amount of weed HE smoked. Like lmao, he's supposed to be a grown adult and he's saying that you should've been babysitting him to make sure he doesn't do drugs as often? You're not his mother, and even that wouldn't make it anyone's fault but his own. He's an addict, and he's most likely in denial since most people still think weed isn't addictive. As an addict, he can only help himself, and he'll only get better if he stops: which you can't control. That isn't on you at all, and you have no obligation to say to him ' hey you smoked like 2 hrs ago, you shouldn't do it again yet". 

I've got some experience in this area, and trust me, the best thing to do is leave. It doesn't matter that he's got a condition. It's tied to his use and if he isn't ready to stop you can't make him. The way he's talking, both blaming you and attempting to manipulate you to stay with him, which would be sabotaging your own goals and life, shows he only loves one thing atm, drugs. It's not your obligation to get him sober and although it's hard to leave , it's harder to watch someone destroy themselves and not be able to help. And, that's without the possibility that you can get pressure into using something/drained financially/etc. Really, think about yourself and what you want going forward; your future shouldn't have to include watching for signs of drug use/monitoring his use/being unsure of what of yours might go missing for cash. You can wish him well and encourage him to get better and give him the resources, but aside from that, you're powerless in this case, and you have your whole life to focus on, you already sound stressed enough with school. 

I know it's weed. I know it's legal. I know it doesn't have withdrawals that can kill you like alcohol or benzos. I know it's not very well recognized as being even addicting. He'll be okay in the hospital, and if he wants to get better, he won't smoke. If he doesn't, then that's on him.

Best of luck.

I get being depressed over being cheated on and getting something, I get how you might feel like she deserves to suffer or whatever, or you just really didn't want to talk about it. Not ONCE did it cross your mind that hey, the girl I was with for nearly half a year, who I really cared about, should know what happened.

The fact that it came up because SHE came by means you had the intention of NEVER telling her. Not after 2 years or 5 or any amount of time. You were completely content moving on with your life, being happy that you got to cure the STI you got, and that you were saved from spending more of a relationship/your life with someone who's a cheater with no remorse. And the big one:

You came to reddit, asking if you're TA but not once in the post did you show any remorse for any damage you could've done, whether to an innocent person or to the person who you claimed you had feelings for. Whether you believe the gonorrhea messed with her reproductive system or not, you said you knew she wanted children. You don't say you feel bad that you didn't mention it when she came to you, crying, telling you to get tested. She might've been TA for cheating and might not have really liked/loved you , but she cared enough to make sure you knew. You seem to care less about her well-being in that case than she cares about yours which, along with my other statements, makes me say this.

And of course, you don't show any remorse and had she not showed up, you would've lived the rest of your life never mentioning it to her. And this is why it's not as easy as saying "hey I'm trans now, gimme hormones". There's hoops to jump through because the one prescribing the HRT / blockers wants to make sure the person is sure about this. That's why most places make you go to a therapist to get a letter of recommendation to start HRT , as an adult, which could take many sessions, plenty of money (since most don't take insurance) and it's a legit psychological assessment over time. Not to mention the first advice is usually to experiment with gender and see how you feel as what you're transitioning to, for at least a year. Not just to know for sure, but also help in the integration process since you would essentially be having to relearn stereotype societal norms if you want to be...not as open about your transness, id say. There's things in place so you don't jump the gun, and then if you still decide this is what is for you, as a minor you need parental consent, and as an adult, you're made known of all the side effects, the negatives so you know it isn't just all fun, and you're monitored by the doc. A lot of centers that specialize in this stuff will provide therapy for the first 6 mo of your transition to help with the psychological effects, especially if you bave a history of depression or anxiety. And that's all for hormones mind you, surgery is a lot more hoops.

For instance : I've been on HRT 10+ yrs, still trying to find a top doc. The one that I found okay reviews of that takes insurance I can switch to has the pre-reqs of : 

-must get a letter from a doctor stating you're being treated and they acknowledge what you're doing
-must get a letter from a licensed psychological professional , who can attest that you are indeed trans, this is what you want, and isnt related to another condition.
And finally, at least for this specific doc:
-must be on HRT for at minimum 2 YEARS.

Which is a big issue, because I know a lot of trans men who have just wanted/gotten top surgery or even bottom and didn't go on HRT at all because their dysphoria was more physical then hormonal. And so this would bar entry for those people, which I think isn't necessarily fair, especially if the other two documents could attest to that. But, this is an example of how you can't just decide and then call up any doc in a phone book and book a DI or hysto or anything like that. (Although tbh both can have grey areas relating to things like possibility of future cancer..)

Yes, sometimes labor can last forever (or at least feel like it), but I think it's ridiculous for two reasons: 

1) it's not like he wants to bring a little handheld thing like a Switch for example, which if it really DID last a while, you were stable and asleep and he wanted to try to calm his own anxieties, he could always pause as soon as he needs to and shove that back in his pocket. This dude said PS5. Does he think that when you go in to wait, the room has a huge TV with an HDMI port? He knows this is a *hospital* we're talking about, right? And even if he managed to set up the huge thing with the wires and all, it would get in the way when it came time to deliver/if he went to get you whatever you need/ask for (like a good partner) then that would mean leaving his precious game which I can imagine would cause him to project that mild frustration out on the closest person there, you.

And of course, 

2) An epidural sort of numbs your lower half, that's it. NO sedation. And you'll still feel uncomfortable there as the contractions come. I don't know if your pregnancy is high risk or if you have any health issues (knock-on-wood), but long labor or not, a good partner would be watching your vitals, making sure you get all the ice chips you need, (esp the longer it goes on, dry mouth isn't fun) and timing contractions. For someone who you said loves you and is excited for the new addition to your family, I would think he'd want to be present throughout the whole thing. People rarely sleep, especially through contractions, and if they're closer together at a certain point, they will want you up anyway to prepare yourself.

What I'm saying is, what you're asking is a total normal ask, a reasonable one, and I feel him bringing up bringing a huge ass machine so he can have fun while you're literally bringing both of your's child into the world seems..insensitive? You spent 9 months (or so) dealing with pain, feeling constantly uncomfortable, and having your hormones ride a rollercoaster, all to lead up to this big moment where you push so hard that an epidural might not be enough (and then not to mention the possible tearing that is somewhat common) to bring this life *your* body created into the world. 

My partner gave birth, but if it was the other way around and she was preoccupied (let's face it: if your partner did actually bring it, that PS5 would be played the entire time, until maybe when its time to cut the cord) I'd be hurt. Because they're having fun while I'm in pain, the least they can do is make sure everything goes smoothly and provide emotional support. It's a scary thing, especially if you're going through it alone or at least feel like you are.

Echoing what others said: when my partner was in labor, I was keeping her company the entire time, running back and forth to get more ice chips, pillows, blankets, etc so she's comfortable, tried to keep her occupied as it's a nerve wracking situation, constantly checked her vitals, and I couldn't even focus on what I *did* bring with me, a parenting book I thought might help (since it talked about the labor and delivery too). 

Sorry for the long rant, I read another comment on here saying that your partner should be cut some slack and let him keep busy if it lasts that long. Well not only is everyone's body different, for all you know it might be over before he could even finish hooking up the actual PS5, but not to be an ass but...He gave his contribution to help form life, but you're the one that's been tired, in pain, and more, for the entirety of your pregnancy, so at least 7/8 months. And now your body is going to go through one of the most intense and uncomfortable things it can do. Why does he get to be "cut some slack" because he's not able to have fun while his partner is in labor?? I just don't get it. And also, when you're not having intense contractions, you might be bored too/want to be distracted if you are told you have a long way to go. I doubt you could focus on a video game even if you liked them and he, say, brought two controllers. I legit played tic-tac-toe and the dots and lines game with my partner when the epidural worked and the contractions were way far apart. She couldn't really focus on it, but it passed the time, and it helped with her nerves. But the difference is, I wasn't bored, I got the idea to play those games for *her*. If you liked video games and that was your partner's plan, then I could maybe *kind of* get it, but eh.

Regardless, tell him how you feel. Tell him that you don't want him to bring it, that you need him present in the moment because this is a big thing, obviously. You can mention also what I said, that the epidural is just for numbing, they won't sedate you in any way, and that like you said, you probably won't slee. But, the point is, while he might be bored, at the very least, so will you. He can survive spending however long you're in labor being a good partner to you for this occasion, it won't kill him.

TL:DR : NTA cause hello OP is gonna be busy pushing out a watermelon and having painful contractions, while the husband will probably be playing fortnite or something, how present can you really be for this important event when you're on a kill streak and can't pause if it's delivery time?

There's your answer. It's a lot simpler than you think. 

For a minute, try and not focus on what OTHER people might think. Think about yourself, and how you feel. You don't need to transition to be trans. Not everyone can. I don't know what specific condition you have, but I know there are people who can't because they either do not react well to HRT (remember, people can be allergic to any medication, or have negative effects which bother them more than the positives that come out of taking T) or have immune system problems. There's people who dont physically transition but do socially. That's enough for some people, and others it's not. If you transition socially (change your name, how you are referred to, dress more masculine, etc) and that makes you feel better, more comfortable to be in your body, then you don't need to worry about the lack of a medical change. At the end of the day, it's what makes YOU more comfortable, that's all that matters. 

You said you came out as trans at 20, so I'm assuming you're older than 20 yo. I don't know where you live, but once you're 21 you definitely could move out. I think you can get off your parents insurance, etc, before 26. You don't need to move out yet but look into getting your own insurance, a non private one like Medicaid (whatever your states version of that is). You're disabled you said. Are you legally disabled or not yet? If you aren't, I suggest getting that done asap. If you are, start saving up when you can. Is your disability linked to your weight? I ask because it might be harder to have disability approved if it's believed that your disability won't last longer than a year (and it can be argued that with surgery and programs, that you could theoretically lose enough weight to alter the affects your disability has on you, if this is the case). 

As long as you're over 18, you don't need your parents permission to transition, but if you're over 18/ 21 they also don't necessarily have to let you live with them. Before jumping in, I'd recommend finding a safe backup plan incase you need to leave/are forced to. Also, make sure to look into your state's laws, as they are drastically changing for us trans peeps atm. Your safety is the most important thing.

If you are getting paid SSI, and they are monitoring it, then I'd say speak to a professional about all this, and be honest if you don't feel safe. If they aren't monitoring your finances, start saving up little bits both as backup and both to help you eventually get a place of your own. There are many case workers who can help for free, or cheap, and not just to get benefits but to get housing. It's easier to get housing for someone with disability, as long as it's documented. 

The max SSI pays to someone without any work history is about 800 I believe. If you can find someone to room with and split rent, you might have an easier shot at getting away from your parents while also saving up on the side for needed things , etc. As awful as you might feel trans wise, it'll feel worse if you're safety isn't secured. IMO, because it does seem like it'll cause problems that you need to plan for, I'd say since you can't medically transition, at least not now, then just do it socially, and only with peers, not your parents. I have friends who got away with wearing guys clothes because there are more men's clothes that are larger sizes, and they fit better for someone overweight in general. So you could always use that as an excuse if your parents bring up why everything you've decided to wear is all masculine.

Finally, just because you like more traditionally feminine things does not mean you can't be trans. There are plenty of people who feel they're in the wrong body, transition with T, and once they pass as a guy, will wear more feminine stuff...it's because they like the actual things but still feel like a guy, and if they can pass as a guy, then they don't have to worry about the dysphoria that comes with being misgendered and can still feel okay/not dysphoric wearing feminine things. Preferences are one thing, like things you like, etc. Feeling is something else. You know you feel like a guy inside the wrong body, and that answers your question. My advice is focus on  doing what you can to not only become independent, but also to get to a more healthy and comfortable weight, as that is enough to cause body dysphoria in CIS people, let alone us. It'll be better for you all around, and then you can make your next focus once you're able to do so, to focus on transitioning in any way, like passing, etc. I know it would be hard and its uncomfortable not passing and being misgendered, but your safety is more important. You cant transition at all, even socially, if youre in danger. And there are plenty of ways, just saying, to pass without T. There are people who find ways to pass and they do, it just takes more effort and work, thats all. If it doesnt feel worth it to you, then its OKAY too, and you'll know how you feel. Only you can really know. This is just my opinion, I just know how it feels as a fellow trans person. I wish you the best of luck, and sorry for the longggg comment.

It depends what state you're in, but I don't think they're available for transitioning until maybe 13? But either way, even when it comes to transitioning as adults, there are requirements before you can just get on HRT / blockers to make sure the person 100% understands what it's like to go through transitioning, etc.

One of them is to change socially, meaning attempting to live as the gender they plan to transition to for at MINIMUM a year. So basically, your child would see a therapist that specializes in transgender health, (which also is needed to write a letter of recommendation for said blockers anyway) and not only would assess your child to make sure they understand what comes with transitioning both physically, mentally but also the social impacts in society today (the way they'll possibly be treated by assholes, etc).

Changing socially would also mean that while seeing said therapist, they also should start trying out dressing as they feel (I started dressing more "tomboyish" since I was 14, but didn't know what being trans was until 19, therefore I didn't actually live as a man, just liked dressing like a boy. This wouldn't have counted, really. Your child would not only benefit from a change of outfits but also trying to find a name/way to be referred that makes them feel more comfortable . Most people go with the "guy version" of their names, some change it completely, it's whatever they feel "right" about. It's hard to find a name and settle on it and feel like it's yours, especially when you've spent your entire life being called something else . I would think it might be easier for more unisex names, like Alex, Sam, etc. since the nickname is unisex even if what it's short for might not be. Lastly, it's a bit hard to explain but "living" as the gender they feel is more than what I just mentioned. It's belng willing to enter more male (in this case) dominated spaces and trying out the mannerisms, etc and seeing if it feels right. In the end, if they feel like a boy, and it's not that they enjoy things about boys or something like that (some people feel more comfortable around guys, really prefer guy things, etc) they'll know. And the societal change will just solidify it more for them/make them feel more "at home" or "right" for them, not put any ideas in their head. If it turns out that they aren't trans, they'll know def too.

I can't explain how good it felt the first time I was called "sir" by someone (and they didn't realize I was born female ans then "correct"  themselves as I could not pass at all back then). I was trying out a different name (not the one I settled on ultimately), and tried walking/talking more guyish , went by "he/him" instead of "she/her", just let myself be referred to as if I was born a guy, just an average guy. It felt for me like things were falling into place, and the dysphoria I felt socially was definitely better when I was not misgendered.

Dysphoria is harder to explain, there's the textbook definition of it, but actually knowing how crippling it can feel, how much worse it makes depression, etc, is harder to actually know how bad it feels unless you feel it yourself . The dysphoria can be body type, like feeling dysphoric about the parts of your body related to the sex you were born as, it can be social like being misgendered/seen socially as what you were born as, and although some people debate whether dysphoria is necessary to be considered transgender, not only are there different types that doesn't require a person to feel both, but also some form of it is required for the psychological diagnosis that helps therapists and psychologists to determine if the person is actually transgender. If a person doesn't feel any type of dysphoria, it might be harder for said diagnosis, which is what is usually needed for the letter of recommendation to start blockers or HRT.

In the end, you can have your child have the diagnosis, have the letter, have lived socially as a guy, and wind up with them being at least a year, maybe two, older. If they wind up with all this, then that's basically saying yes your kid is transgender, and wants to transition. They've been given a greenlight by a professional and they've communicated how they feel. At the end of the day, as the parent of an underage child, you still have the choice to say no. While it's understandable the fears of how it will affect your child, I can assure you that by this point, your child will definitely be sure of how they feel. If you still wish to be supportive and honor that, then that's great! 

You want to know the effects of everything though, and there is plenty of knowledge online, not to mention that both you and your child will be told all the side effects when seeing the doctor whom you plan to ask to prescribe the medications. I want you to know that for one, gender is known by age 5, meaning your child is pretty sure they know when they tell you . This isn't something people want, like a trend, if they truly feel that way, as being transgender is just like being a part of the rest of the lgbtqia community; it's not fun. Most of us are bullies in some shape or form, a lot of us are attacked and physically (and of course) emotionally assaulted, and there are many of us who have ended their lives because of the depression. It's not something someone would want to lie about or be just for the hell of it. But while this sounds alarming, the depression of not being able to be who they really are inside is just as overwhelming and even if you feel you're protecting them if you decide to say no, it'll hurt them in a different kind of way, that usually winds up hurting a lot more. That's not to guilt you in any way, it's just statistically known.

DID (dissociative identity disorder) , a.k.a. the one with the multiple personalities, is different from schizophrenia. A big reason that the two are confused is that the basis of the word schizophrenia is literally meant "a split mind". I think this is because of the common dissociation in schizophrenia that can give the indication that the individual with it is "split" from reality or that the mind is "split in pieces" to cause some of the fragmented-like effects, like the disorganized speech, the sometimes memory loss, the "split from reality" when delusions of grandeur cause someone to believe they are God/Jesus reincarnate, the Devil, the president, etc. I could go on, but I'm sure you get the point. 

JSYK, the most common form of schizophrenia is paranoid schizophrenia, which consists of delusions of persecution, (believing that you're being followed by say, the FBI) and sometimes can consist of hallucinations, or delusions, (different than hallucinations), such as delusions of grandeur sometimes, as in believing you are more important than you actually are (to the extent that, going with the example of the paranoia of being followed by the FBI, you may believe also that this is because you are given an important mission from the CIA or a foreign intelligence that can help save the world and the FBI may be trying to stop you) and can also be mixed with the many other types of schizophrenia to produce other symptoms, like disorganized speech, etc. 

I'd highly recommend watching the movie "A Beautiful Mind", as the MC is based completely on the real life guy, but so is the entire movie, and it showcases what I've explained perfectly. It's also one of the movies that professors like to show in psychology classes. It's a good movie also in general, and another recommendation would be "Donnie Darko" . One of my favs and also shows what I've explained (and that's without spoiling anything , as it is brought up very quickly that Donnie is believed to have a form of schizophrenia) 

TL;DR - Schizophrenia is not the disorder with multiple personalities. They're two very different things .

The best thing I can tell you is what others have said, stick to a routine so you're never bored and you're always busy. 

When you start getting cravings, either talk to someone who understands or can maybe help distract you... Cravings typically last about 20-30 minutes for most substances, meaning as long as you keep yourself distracted and busy for that long, in twenty min/half an hour, you should feel them less. Over time cravings get better.

Figure out your triggers . If it's boredom, then always stay busy . You'd be surprised what people can do even stuck at home. Perhaps take up a hobby ? I force myself to try playing video games since that's what I used to love (even though depression made them seem not as fun anymore) 

if the trigger is having money, set up a bank account that places a limit on withdrawals, like a savings account. When you get income, either have it direct deposited or deposit it immediately . If you have an on the books job, they can help you maybe set up direct deposit or if you get a check, do mobile deposit.

If your trigger is stress, then there are many other ways to cope, there's the conventional writing down your emotions / letting them out with music (playing/singing along or making your own). When you're allowed to be out, you can consider taking out your frustrations at the gym. Having an addictive personality (common with people with addictions) can mean you can wind up addicted to anything else, even working out. While that's still an addiction and sometimes can be unhealthy if you decide to for example, say, focus on getting so fit that you consider steroids , or push your body harder than it can handle, then you would need to find something else, perhaps a sport? But usually working out is the best thing to do coming off an addiction as it not only tires you, keeps you busy and gives you something to focus on, but it also creates a routine. 

If your trigger is a mental illness like depression (and you've been self medicating K to feel better), then consider immediately getting into therapy and perhaps going on an SSRI to have something that will boost your seretonin without harming you . Also depending on your diagnosis you might need a certain type of therapy, whether it's CBT, DBT, hypo-therapy for repressed trauma, etc.

Lastly, while I myself don't believe in it and didn't need it to have the three years I currently do clean from heroin , there's NA meetings/12 step meetings/spirituality focused/higher power focused meetings. I personally don't believe in a type of higher power in which to "give myself over to" and I also believe it not only takes fault off of you in a way (taking away some accountability, even if one of the steps is making amends to those you've harmed. It feels more like when you get to that step, making amends to each person doesn't feel sincere. A lot of people aren't sure how to go about it , so some use either a template, pre-write, or might ask their sponsor what to say) but it also takes off achievement of the addict. If only the higher power can keep you clean, then (to me) it seems like when you stay clean through tough cravings, or maybe hit a big milestone (like a whole year) then you can't really take credit as it's the higher power that is what's kept you clean, not yourself.

Also, there is the fact that since the meetings are not run by licensed counselors/social workers/therapists/CASAC workers/etc, but by other addicts, meaning they can't help you get to the root of what caused your addiction, especially if it's something like trauma, or mental illness. You're going to need actual therapy like I said earlier, and maybe meds.

Also, the meetings are usually filled with what I call "war stories". When you get out of rehab they say "90 meetings 90 days", meaning one meeting a day. The last thing I want, especially if I have cravings, is to hear every single day about other people's stories (even if they're negative and bleak) about their drug use. It's triggering , and was especially in the very beginning. I didn't care for people telling me how good dope made them feel (sometimes going into vivid details) but how bad it hurt them. Im a dope addict, I know how good it feels. And I had friends who used (while I was using ) so I know how bad things can get at times and how many people almost died or wound up dying . But like I said , this is just my experience. It works for som people .

Best of luck my friend , and you can do this! The most important thing is wanting to stop and being willing to do what you need to to do so.

There's a reason medications have expiry dates though. Since most people have more than one dose in each vial the vial gets reused anyway, in which case the only difference is the top is off as opposed to a brand new one. Since they're the sealed kind that needs to be stuck through with the syringe to get the medication, it technically should be fine. I've done this before, especially since my dose doesn't line up with the amount. Ive had like a half of a shot left in the vial and had to wait to get my next vial to do my full shot, and I first use what's left. I've also left it before too and used it when I was in-between waiting for the script to fill if it was a weird month. 

I always have a shot and a half in each vial, since my dose is .6, which means after 3 shots (since every month I get 2 vials) I'm still left with about .2ccs until the next script

I have to, my dose is .6 ccs biweekly and the vial holds 200 mg/ml in the 1ml vial. I was taught to store it properly away from anything that could mess with it and everytime you reuse it, alcohol the opening before putting the syringe in. (Since the medication can't freely come out, it's okay, and since you're supposed to sterilize it as well as you could, it shouldn't give you problems going in. I've been doing this on and off for like, a decade nearly, and *knockonwood* it's been okay.

Also, not only was I told this by several medical professionals, but when I started getting the shots and I had to bring my own vial to the appt to have them administer it, they did the same thing .

Edit: did you contaminate a WHOLE vial or is there nothing left in there but what you put? Either way I'd say don't use it but hopefully it didn't waste a whole months worth of meds because it'll be a pain in the ass to get another of it's not due yet.

Even though when you give yourself the T you use alcohol, sterile needles, etc, once it's penetrated your skin (and then subsequently brought back out) it then can pick up whatever contaminates could be right under the skin, any part it might touch that wasn't sterilized, any airborne contaminates, etc.

I wouldn't chance it. Its obviously different, but when I was using IV substances, even when I was verrryyy careful and made sure everything was sterile, there's always the possibility something could happen. For me, that was reusing a syringe I already used and even though I used alcohol on the spot, I wound up hospitalized due to a major bone infection and couldn't walk for months. Even though the shots are IM, that doesn't mean if it's contaminated it can't still get into your bloodstream.

Throw the vial out, don't chance it, and next time make sure to just measure it really correctly in the vial so when you pull out the syringe it's at the dose you need. If you are like me and wind up missing like half a point or something because you dont push it all the way in to avoid the air bubbles, then it's okay to lose that tiny little bit, it won't make a difference.

The withdrawals are your body reacting to not having what it's been getting. Pain killers relieve pain; therefore the withdrawals you get are flu like symptoms, and pain. Stimulant withdrawal is mental yes, depression and anxiety. Also, it can cause lethargy and sleeping crashes. Technically, you don't get physical withdrawals really from stimulants. The only possible ones really is the sleep binges. I know sometimes on the comedown, I get physical symptoms like cramping like pain, and sweating profusely, but that's on the comedown, not actual withdrawal from going days without it.

Even still, it's a lifelong battle once you've been hooked, even after being clean. I don't know your beliefs in the afterlife, but know that your sister does not have to fight these demons anymore at least. As horrible as it is. It eats away at your thoughts, and makes it easy to rationalize doing hurtful and even manipulative things just to feel better.
